property_summary: For any caller and any value, calling SetMinSum(...) on the reference contract always succeeds (does not revert) exactly once per uninitialized contract and sets MinSum to the provided value; removing the locked_ state updates in the modifier allows a reentrant attacker to call SetMinSum multiple times during the same transaction causing MinSum to end up different (the buggy version can be re-entered and thus allows MinSum to be changed unexpectedly).

For any caller and any value, calling SetMinSum(x) on the correct contract either (a) sets MinSum to x and prevents any nested reentrant call from changing it within the same transaction (due to nonReentrant_ locking), so after the top-level call finishes MinSum == x; the mutant removes the locking state update, allowing a reentrant attacker to call SetMinSum(y) during the outer call and leave MinSum != x for some inputs.

For any caller and any uint value v passed to SetMinSum(v), the reference contract always finishes the external call with MinSum == v (non-reentrant: nested SetMinSum cannot change it during the same transaction); the mutant that omits the locking updates allows a re-entrant attacker to call back into SetMinSum during the outer call and leave MinSum != v for some fuzzed v and attacker scenario.

For any uint x and any attacker address, calling SetMinSum(x) on the correct contract always results in c.MinSum() == x after the call completes (non-reentrancy prevents nested SetMinSum from changing it), whereas the mutant that omits locked_ state updates allows a reentrant attacker to re-enter SetMinSum during the outer call and leave MinSum != x for some fuzzed x and attacker behavior.

For every input value v and any attacker, a call to SetMinSum(v) on the reference contract always results in c.MinSum() == v after the call completes (nonReentrant_ prevents nested SetMinSum from changing it); the mutant that removes the locking updates allows a reentrant attacker to call back into SetMinSum during the outer call and cause c.MinSum() != v for some inputs.

For any caller and any value, calling SetMinSum on the correct contract always sets MinSum to the provided value (and call does not revert if contract not yet initialized); removing the reentrancy guard can allow a reentrant attacker to change contract state such that after SetMinSum returns the stored MinSum differs — the mutant can be exploited by a reentrant callee to make MinSum not equal the argument passed.

For any caller and any uint256 x, after calling SetMinSum(x) on the correct contract C (when not yet initialized) the public MinSum equals x; removing the nonReentrant_ guard allows a reentrant attacker (deployed helper) to call back during SetMinSum and change contract state so that after SetMinSum returns MinSum != x for some inputs.

For any caller and any uint256 v, calling SetMinSum(v) on the correct contract (when not initialized) stores MinSum == v after the call returns; the mutant (no-op nonReentrant_) can be exploited by a reentrant attacker to change MinSum during the call so that after SetMinSum returns MinSum != v for some inputs.

For any caller and any uint256 v, calling SetMinSum(v) on the reference contract (when not yet initialized) always results in c.MinSum() == v after the call returns; removing the nonReentrant_ guard allows a reentrant attacker (deployed helper) to call back and change MinSum during execution so that after SetMinSum returns MinSum() != v for some inputs.

For any caller and any uint256 x, calling SetMinSum(x) on the reference (with nonReentrant_ active) always completes without reentrancy so MinSum equals x afterwards; the mutant (nonReentrant_ a no-op) can be exploited by a reentrant callee that re-enters during SetMinSum to change MinSum so that after the call returns MinSum != x for some inputs.

After calling SetLogFile(x) the contract's Log getter should equal the address x (i.e., SetLogFile stores the provided address); the mutant clears Log to address(0) so this rule is violated for inputs where x != address(0).

For any non-zero address provided to SetLogFile, the reference contract stores that address as Log (so address(c.Log()) == provided), whereas the mutant clears Log to address(0) breaking this rule for some inputs.

For every address a, calling SetLogFile(a) on the correct contract stores that address as the Log file (address(c.Log()) == a); the mutant instead stores address(0) (so for any a != address(0) the property is violated).

For any caller-provided nonzero address A, calling SetLogFile(A) on the correct contract stores A as the Log file (address(c.Log()) == A); the mutant instead clears Log to address(0), so this property is violated for some inputs (A != address(0)).

For any address X passed to SetLogFile by any caller before initialization, the correct contract stores X as the Log file (address(c.Log()) == X) while the mutant writes address(0) instead, so there exist inputs (any X != address(0)) that make the mutant disagree with this rule.

After calling SetLogFile(addr) from any caller, the reference contract always sets the Log file address to the provided addr (call succeeds and c.Log() == addr), but the buggy variant (missing locked_ = true) can be re-entered during SetLogFile by a malicious callee which calls back into SetLogFile and cause the final stored Log to differ for some inputs (the property: c.Log() equals the last SetLogFile argument and call returns successfully).

Invariant: after any successful call to SetLogFile(x) from any caller, the contract's Log getter returns x (the reference sets the value deterministically); the mutant that omits setting locked_ = true allows a reentrant attacker to change Log during the call so that this invariant can be violated for some inputs.

For any caller and any address arg, a completed call to SetLogFile(x) on the correct contract always results in c.Log() == x (the log pointer equals the argument); removing the setting of locked_ = true lets a malicious callee re-enter during SetLogFile and change the final stored Log, violating this rule for some fuzzed inputs.

For every caller and any address argument, a successful call to SetLogFile(x) on the reference contract never reverts (completes) and leaves c.Log() equal to x; the mutant that omits setting locked_ = true allows a reentrant attacker (whose fallback calls back into SetLogFile) to cause a later reentrant SetLogFile to run and leave c.Log() different after the original call completes, so there exist inputs (attacker address and initial caller) that make c.Log() differ — the test deploys an attacker contract that reenters during SetLogFile to detect this.

For any caller and any target address, a completed call to SetLogFile(target) on the correct contract always leaves the public Log getter equal to target (the reference prevents reentrant updates during the call); the mutant that omits setting locked_ = true allows a reentrant attacker to change Log during SetLogFile so some inputs produce a different final Log.

For any caller, after calling Initialized() the contract's public boolean flag 'intitalized' becomes true; the mutant flips it to false so there exist inputs where the flag is not true after the call.

For every caller and input, calling Initialized() on the correct contract sets the public boolean intitalized to true; the mutant sets it to false, so there exist calls where the post-call getter differs (true vs false).

For every caller and for any prior state, invoking Initialized() on the correct contract always makes the public flag intitalized become true (so subsequent reads of the public getter return true); the mutant sets it to false, so there exist inputs where the post-call getter is false, violating the rule.

For every caller and prior state, calling Initialized() always results in the public boolean intitalized being true (the reference sets it to true; the mutant sets it to false and thus violates this rule for some inputs).

For any caller and any prior state, calling Initialized() on the reference contract sets the public boolean intitalized to true (so the getter returns true); the mutant sets it to false, so there exist calls where the post-call getter is false, violating this rule.

For any caller and any prior state, calling Initialized() on the correct contract always succeeds (does not revert) and sets the public bool 'intitalized' to true; the mutant that never resets locked_ will cause subsequent calls to revert (or leave intitalized false) for some inputs due to the reentrancy lock remaining set.

For any caller and any sequence, calling Initialized() on the correct contract always succeeds (does not revert) and sets C.intitalized to true; the mutant that fails to reset the reentrancy lock can cause Initialized() to revert (or leave intitalized false) for some sequences/inputs involving two successive calls, which the fuzzer can find.

For any single external caller and any initial state, calling Initialized() on the correct contract always succeeds (does not revert) and sets the public bool intitalized to true; the mutant that omits resetting the reentrancy lock can cause Initialized() to revert (or subsequent calls to fail) for some adversarial callee interactions, so there exist inputs where the mutant does not set intitalized while the reference does.

For any caller and any admissible setup, a single call to Initialized() on the correct contract always returns successfully and sets the public bool intitalized to true; the mutant that fails to reset the reentrancy lock can leave locked_ = true and cause Initialized() to revert (or be uncallable) in a subsequent invocation through an adversarial external call path, so there exist inputs where the reference reports intitalized==true while the mutant does not allow that.

For any caller and any prior state, a single call to Initialized() on the correct contract always succeeds (does not revert) and results in the public bool intitalized becoming true; the mutant that omits resetting the reentrancy lock can cause Initialized() to revert (or be blocked) for some sequences/inputs so that intitalized remains false — therefore: after calling Initialized() once, c.intitalized() must be true on the reference but may be false on the mutant for some fuzzed inputs.

After any successful Put call by an account, the account's recorded balance in C decreases only when that account later successfully Collects — in particular, a subsequent Put from the same account always leaves the contract still callable (nonReentrant unlocked) so the account can perform another Put; the mutant that never resets locked_ will make subsequent external calls into C (e.g., a second Put) revert due to reentrancy lock, breaking the rule for some inputs.

For any caller and any deposit amount/lockTime, calling Put twice in a row (two separate external transactions) succeeds on the correct contract (nonReentrant resets) but the mutant that fails to unlock will make the second Put revert for some inputs; the test fuzzes caller, amount and lockTime and checks that two consecutive Put calls both succeed on the reference.

For any caller and any admissible deposit (value) and lockTime, after a successful Put by that caller the contract remains callable by other distinct callers (i.e., a different attacker/account can still successfully call Put); the mutant that never releases the reentrancy lock can leave the contract permanently locked after one call, preventing some other caller from calling Put.

For any caller, a single successful external Put call that completes does not permanently lock the contract: immediately after that call, a fresh Put from a different caller with a small nonzero value must still be accepted (succeed) on the reference, whereas the mutant that never clears locked_ will make that subsequent Put fail for some fuzzed inputs.

After any successful call to Put by an address that triggers an external call to a callee (via Log.AddMessage which calls an external contract address previously set by SetLogFile), the reference contract always allows a subsequent Put from the same caller to succeed (nonReentrant is released), while the mutant that never resets locked_ can leave the contract locked and make that subsequent Put revert when Log.AddMessage is an external contract that itself makes an external call back (or simply returns normally) — so two sequential transactions from the same caller (with a real contract as Log) always both succeed on the reference but can fail on the mutant.

For any caller, calling Put(v) increases that caller's stored Acc[msg.sender].balance by v (i.e., new balance = old balance + msg.value); the mutant omits adding msg.value so for some inputs the stored balance does not increase by the sent amount.

For any caller and any positive msg.value, after calling Put(lock) the caller's stored Acc[msg.sender].balance increases by exactly the sent msg.value (i.e., new balance >= msg.value and specifically delta == msg.value when starting from zero); the mutant that omits adding msg.value will violate this for some inputs (e.g., when starting balance is zero and msg.value>0).

For any caller and any nonzero Ether value sent to Put, the caller's recorded Acc[msg.sender].balance increases by at least the sent msg.value (i.e., after Put the stored balance >= previous balance + msg.value); the mutant that omits adding msg.value can violate this by leaving the stored balance unchanged.

For any caller and any sent Ether value, after calling Put(...) the contract's logged last message records the sent value (LastMsg.Val == msg.value); the mutant still logs msg.value but fails to update stored balance, so checking that address(c).balance increased by the sent amount distinguishes them (reference: contract balance increases by msg.value when Put is called payable; mutant: contract balance still increases but stored Acc balance doesn't — however since contract's ETH balance always increases in both, instead we assert that Acc(msg.sender).balance >= msg.value after Put when starting from zero, which holds for the reference but fails for the mutant.

For any caller and any nonzero Ether value sent to Put when their prior recorded balance is zero, after Put the caller's Acc[msg.sender].balance is strictly equal to the sent msg.value; the mutant that omits adding msg.value breaks this (leaving balance zero).

After any Put by an account that already has a nonzero balance, the reference contract preserves and increases the stored Acc[addr].balance by msg.value (i.e., new balance == old + msg.value), whereas the mutant overwrites and sets balance == msg.value for some inputs (accounts with existing balance).

For any caller and any msg.value, a successful Put increases that caller's stored balance by exactly msg.value (new balance == old balance + msg.value); the mutant that overwrites acc.balance breaks this when caller already had nonzero balance.

For any caller and any sent value, after a successful Put the caller's stored Acc balance equals its previous stored balance plus msg.value (i.e., Put is additive); the mutant that overwrites acc.balance breaks this rule when the caller already had a nonzero prior balance.

For any caller and any nonzero msg.value, calling Put increases the caller's stored Acc balance by at least the sent msg.value (i.e., new balance >= old balance) — the mutant that overwrites acc.balance with msg.value can decrease balance when prior balance > 0, violating this.

For any caller and any sent value, if the caller's prior stored balance is zero then after Put the stored balance equals msg.value (the reference preserves this, while the mutant can only match this for zero prior balance but will diverge for nonzero prior balances); we use this with an admissible domain requiring prior balance == 0 so the reference always satisfies it and the mutant still can be distinguished when the fuzzer chooses a caller that first gets a nonzero balance then calls Put again (the mutant will fail the additive behavior while the reference preserves it).

After any Put by an account with given _lockTime and value, the holder's unlockTime in the reference is always based on block.timestamp (so unlockTime >= block.timestamp) whereas the mutant sometimes sets unlockTime based on block.number which can be much smaller than block.timestamp causing unlockTime < block.timestamp for some inputs (i.e., unlockTime < block.timestamp can occur under the mutant but never in the reference).

For any caller, after calling Put(_lockTime) with some msg.value the holder's unlockTime in the correct contract is always >= block.timestamp (because it is set using block.timestamp + _lockTime), whereas the mutant that uses block.number can produce an unlockTime that is < block.timestamp for some inputs (block.number + _lockTime may be less than the current timestamp) — the test checks unlockTime >= block.timestamp after Put.
